subject: Pathology
summary: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a ubiquitous herpesvirus that infects B cells, causing infectious mononucleosis and driving oncogenesis in diseases like Burkitt lymphoma. It establishes lifelong latency and reactivates under immune stress.

sections.p: EBV is a double‑stranded DNA herpesvirus that infects >90% of people worldwide, usually in childhood. Primary infection may be silent or present as infectious mononucleosis; the virus then persists in memory B cells.
b: Transmitted by saliva, rarely by blood or organ transplant

sections.p: EBV infects epithelial cells and CD21‑positive B lymphocytes. It expresses latency proteins (EBNA, LMP) that drive B‑cell proliferation and evade immune detection.
b: Latency III (full) in naïve B cells, latency I in memory B cells

sections.p: Virus spreads through intimate saliva contact. After entry, it infects oropharyngeal epithelium, then B cells where it establishes latency. Reactivation can occur with immunosuppression.
b: No airborne spread; safe to use standard precautions

sections.p: EBV causes a spectrum from self‑limited infectious mononucleosis to malignancies (Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma) and rare complications like splenic rupture.
b: Infectious mononucleosis: fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, atypical lymphocytes
Endemic Burkitt lymphoma: jaw or abdominal mass, c‑myc translocation t(8;14)
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma: nasal obstruction, epistaxis, cervical nodes

sections.p: Combine clinical picture with serology, hematology, and, when needed, tissue pathology.
b: If serology unavailable, rely on clinical triad + CBC and consider PCR for EBV DNA

t.b: Confirms recent EBV infection; positive in 80% of adolescents, may be negative early or in children
Distinguishes acute (VCA‑IgM+, VCA‑IgG+, EBNA‑) from past infection (VCA‑IgG+, EBNA+)
Lymphocytosis with >10% atypical lymphocytes supports mononucleosis; severe anemia or leukopenia may suggest lymphoma
Shows EBV‑positive Reed‑Sternberg cells (Hodgkin) or c‑myc translocation (Burkitt); definitive for malignancy

sections.p: No antiviral cures EBV; management is supportive for mononucleosis and oncologic therapy for malignancies.
b: Supportive care: analgesics, hydration, avoid contact sports for 4 weeks to prevent splenic rupture
Corticosteroids only for airway obstruction or severe hemolysis
Burkitt lymphoma: combination chemotherapy (e.g., cyclophosphamide‑based) plus supportive growth factors

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams.
b: Positive heterophile test + atypical lymphocytes = infectious mononucleosis
Endemic Burkitt lymphoma = EBV + chronic malaria; look for jaw mass and t(8;14)
EBV latency patterns dictate oncogenic potential

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden abdominal pain with signs of splenic rupture
Unexplained rapidly enlarging lymph node mass

faq.q: Why does EBV cause a sore throat?
faq.a: Infected epithelial cells and reactive lymphoid tissue become inflamed, producing pharyngitis.
No vaccine exists; avoid sharing drinks or utensils with infected individuals during acute illness.
Usually mild, but can trigger lymphoproliferative disease in immunocompromised patients.

exam: Explain the serologic pattern that distinguishes acute EBV infection from past exposure.
Describe the pathogenesis linking chronic malaria, EBV, and endemic Burkitt lymphoma.
List three clinical features that help differentiate infectious mononucleosis from bacterial pharyngitis.
